entries.content:
Jonathan Chait on the White House Correspondents’ Dinner, the attacks on Barack Obama’s legacy, and the Michigan Democratic Senate primary that will decide the future of the party. Plus: more Trump tariffs and Eric Cline’s 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed.

Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube

In this week’s episode of The David Frum Show, The Atlantic’s David Frum opens with his reaction to President Trump’s latest round of tariffs and explains why he believes they are weakening America’s economy and its alliances.

Then, David is joined by his Atlantic colleague Jonathan Chait for a wide-ranging discussion on the White House Correspondents’ Dinner, whether presidents should be funny, the growing attacks on Barack Obama’s legacy, and the battle in Michigan between moderates and the progressive left that could shape the Democratic Party’s future.

Finally, David closes the show with a discussion of Eric Cline’s 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed and the Bronze Age collapse.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

David Frum: You are kind of an immoderate centrist. You’re ready to—you have centrist views, but you’re ready to brawl. But do you see, as you look at the Democratic Party, that there’s something about the moderate—they will not fight back? And therefore, they’re abdicating by default to people who are going to end up empowering Trump. And whoever Trump’s successor is, probably J. D. Vance, and all that J. D. Vance means for the future of American democracy.

Chait: Absolutely. Look, it’s, it’s an old problem, right? The definition of a liberal is someone who’s too broad-minded to take his own side in an argument. This has been something that liberals have noticed about ourselves and have been complaining about ourselves, without doing anything to change, for generations.

[Music]

David Frum: Welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be my Atlantic colleague Jonathan Chait, and we’ll be talking about Obama’s legacy and what it means for the future of American politics. The book this week will be 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed by Eric Cline, a study of the end of the Bronze Age.

But before either my dialogue with Jonathan Chait or the book discussion, some opening thoughts on the most recent rounds of tariff announcements by President Trump. Last Friday, President Trump announced his latest tariffs to go into effect. He targeted 60 economies. I say “60 economies,” because one of the 60 targeted was Taiwan, which is not regarded by the United States as a country but only as an economy. So, 60 economies including Taiwan; 59 countries plus Taiwan.

The ostensible basis of this new round of tariff increases was to combat forced labor. President Trump used a provision in American law that allows the president power to impose tariffs on countries that use forced or slave labor, and he said: That’s it. In order to fight forced or slave labor, these 60 economies, including Taiwan, are going to be targeted by a new round of tariff increases.

The grounds given for the tariffs are not really very plausible. There is no or barely any factual showing that all of these 60 were engaged in some way in forced labor. The United States, after all, is not completely clean on this question either, and there’s no graduation of the tariff to the alleged cause. There’s no saying: Such-and-such country has more forced labor or more openness to forced labor, such-and-such has less; therefore they have different tariff rates. No. It’s just—we accuse these 60 economies, we target them with tariffs, and we’re doing this even though our own hands are not clean. The United States economy is open in many ways to forced labor.

Pretty obviously, what is going on here is that Trump is looking for some legal basis to reinstate the tariffs that he has had struck down in the past. President Trump originally used an emergency economic authority from the 1970s. The Supreme Court told him he couldn’t do it. Then he fell back on a temporary provision that allowed him to impose tariffs for a period of time, I think 150 days, and that time has run out. So now he’s looking for what he can get.

As the president returns again and again and again to imposing tariffs on the world, a question has to be asked: What on earth could any Trump supporter imagine the president is possibly doing that is, in any way, in the American national interest? The emotional basis, the argumentative basis, the intellectual basis for tariffs is that we are supposedly reindustrializing the United States. But since Donald Trump has become president, manufacturing jobs in the United States have declined by the tens of thousands, probably somewhere between 80,000 and 100,000 net manufacturing jobs fewer as I record in the summer of 2026 than when Donald Trump became president at the beginning of 2025.

Because other sectors other employment sectors are continuing to grow, especially health care, this loss of a net 100,000 manufacturing jobs means that manufacturing as a share of nonfarm payrolls has now dipped below 8 percent, which is the lowest level that manufacturing has had in American employment since figures began. Maybe it was lower in 1776 than it is now, but since good figures began, this is the lowest. It’s a record. So obviously, it’s not working. And it’s not just jobs that are being lost. Manufacturing output and manufacturing investment also seem to be in decline. This is a little harder to calculate because there’s a huge capital-investment boom going on because of artificial-intelligence data centers. A lot of money is being committed to these data centers, and the question is: To what extent does this get counted as manufacturing investment and whatnot? But private economists who have tried to separate out seem to be in some kind of agreement that, at best, manufacturing investment is flat in the Trump year and a half, maybe down a little bit, because of the problem of the Trump tariffs.

The thing I wish I could pound into the head of tariff supporters is that every tariffed item is not only a product that you sell to consumers; it’s also an input into something else. When you impose tariffs on goods, you make not just things more expensive for American consumers—you make things more expensive for the American companies that buy those things and put them into other things. It’s a house-that-Jack-built problem. Every time you make an input more expensive, you make the ultimate product more expensive and make the final American product that much less competitive on world markets. And the result is: You can’t compete, so you sell less, so you invest less, so you employ less.

A large part of the attraction of tariffs to Donald Trump seems to be that they appeal to his desire for dominance. His perception of the world is divided into subjects and into enemies, and if you’re not a subject, then you’re an enemy. And if you’re an enemy, then there are no rules. And if you’re a subject, for that matter, there aren’t any rules either. That everything is an expression of will and ego, and all economics is a matter of I win, you lose, and if I don’t feel I’m winning, then I must be losing.

This has become the signature political and economic philosophy of an entire political party under Donald Trump. The party that used to stand for markets and enterprise, the Republican Party, the party of Reagan and Romney. We’re on a bad track here, and these latest tariffs mark another bad milestone on that bad track. We need to get off this, and we need to start creating in freedom and with rules.

That doesn’t mean that we pretend that China is not a problem. China is a problem, and there’s forced labor in China. And China is a rule-breaker and steals intellectual property. You need a China-specific solution to the problem of trade, not a solution that destroys the whole apparatus of trade with all of America’s friends and, increasingly, former friends.

The United States is now bound in a grinding and frustrating war with Iran. It needs all the friends it can get. The idea that it is waging economic aggression on all of its partners and then acting baffled and befuddled that these partners don’t help out on the Iran problem—a war that the United States started and that it did not have to start and that now it can’t get out of—that just, again, seems to be another bad milestone on another bad path.

The way out of all of America’s problems—it’s not the whole solution, but it’s the beginning of a solution—is to return to the path of free and fair trade with friendly-minded nations, bracketing China as a special problem, and otherwise dropping tariffs to the lowest rates possible and returning to the days when the United States negotiated agreements with its friends to trade in freedom and prosperity with mutual benefit and understanding that true trade makes all those who participate in it better off.

And now my dialogue with Jonathan Chait.

[Music]

Frum: Jonathan Chait has dedicated 30 years as one of this country’s sharpest, wittiest, and most ornery advocates for liberalism, first at The New Republic, then at New York magazine, and since 2024 at The Atlantic. It’s a remarkable career made more impressive by the fact that journalism was always his second choice of avocation, adopted only after the involuntary abandonment of his true ambition: head coach of the University of Michigan football team.

Jonathan Chait is the author of Audacity: How Barack Obama Defied His Critics and Created a Legacy That Will Prevail. And Jonathan is a continuing reminder that liberalism doesn’t have to be apologetic or bashful about itself. Jonathan, welcome to The David Frum Show.

Jonathan Chait: Thank you, David.

Frum: Okay, so we have a number of things to talk about today. I want to start—I know this is a topic that’s maybe a little more interesting to me than to you—but to start by looking back at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner that was recorded on Saturday night, just a few days before you and I record. This has always been a kind of troublesome event from a point of view of Washington journalism. There are big advantages to being close to politicians, and big hazards as well. So I know you worked at the glory days of The New Republic when there was a lot of intimacy between The New Republic and the politicians it liked. How do you think about events like the White House Correspondents’ Dinner? And do you think about them differently in the age of Trump from the way you thought about them before?

Chait: I was always very skeptical of these events. I went to one to see what it was like, but I felt like if you go to more than one, then you’re no longer going anthropologically; you’re actually part of the thing. And I didn’t want to be part of the thing, because I think it’s a little bit gross. Part of it, just mechanically, is journalistic outlets using themselves as intermediaries for their advertisers to give them access to politicians and to celebrities. The celebrities come because they get some cachet for being at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner. The politicians get access to donors and to celebrities and to journalists. And I feel like it’s cozy for everyone, but I don’t think it’s really good for the journalism profession at all, and never has been.

In the Trump era, people have started to question it more than they have, but I feel like The New York Times was correct 20-some years ago to pull out of the event, and I wish everyone else would too.

Frum: Trump has changed the ritual in one very noticeable way—which was, in the past, the president’s speech always followed a strict form. Which was a series of gentle jibes at the press, somewhat tougher jibes at himself, occasional jibes at political opponents. That was handled with extreme care. Obama did them more than others, but that was always a little dangerous to do because it sort of violated the treaty of the evening. Followed, of course, by the moment at the end where the politician switches from humor to seriousness and pays tribute to the important role of the press, and everyone likes hearing him say it, whatever the politician may think in the recesses of the politician’s heart.

Trump just goes on pure aggression, pure attack. And that may make it easier for journalists to disavow or disconnect themselves from something that was troublesome before.

Chait: I think that’s right. What was the most revealing joke he made was actually a decent joke, at least on paper. His delivery was horrible, because he can’t deliver written text. But he made a joke about how he’s basically taken control of CBS News, how he effectuated regime change there and installed Bari Weiss. And that’s actually pretty chilling, right? I mean, that’s the [Viktor] Orbán playbook that we were all warning about in action, and he’s just boasting about it to the faces of the journalists.

Frum: It’s also, by the way, self-defeating in a way that Trump’s speeches are often not very strategic. But if it were true that Bari Weiss was the person you had installed at CBS, that is the last joke in the world that a president should make, because it only detracts from the effectiveness of your supposed ally. Which I, again, I don’t think she is. But if she were, it detracts from your effectiveness. It undercuts her. It puts her in an untenable situation. Why would you say such a thing? Trump doesn’t seem always to think those things through

Chait: Well, he doesn’t think them through. But I think at some level he’s acting from some instinct to dominate and to make everyone acknowledge the domination, right? He doesn’t work with any subtlety. He actually has to tell people what he’s done and force them to wear the hat on their head.

We may not want to go down this path of debating what’s happened at CBS, but I think it’s pretty clear that Trump believes he has done this at CBS. Now, whether Bari Weiss thinks that’s what she’s doing is a different question.

Frum: I think you make a very shrewd point. Which is that Trump, even when he would do better to allow dignity to people whom he thinks of as allies—he can’t do it. He has to humiliate; he has to dominate. He has to actually take his friend’s head and dump it in the bucket of shit, and pull the friend’s head out again and say, See, my friend is now covered in shit thanks to me. That’s the kind of guy I am, and this is the kind of low-grade character my friend is.

Chait: That’s right. That’s right. I mean, bending the knee is a metaphor people often use, but there’s a visual strikingness to it, right? I mean, an actual sign of submission is what he requires of people who submit to him.

David Frum: Now, let me pivot here to the Barack Obama first White House correspondent dinners, and then his presidency. When I wrote speeches for President [George] W. Bush, I occasionally tried to introduce jokes into them. I have this especially vivid memory of writing a joke that—I’m now going to forget what the joke is, unfortunately. But I remember thinking it was quite good, and putting it into a speech, and having the joke be struck by [senior adviser] Karl Rove personally. And when I went to Karl Rove to complain and say the joke was funny, Rove said—and I thought this was very wise—he said, The joke was funny. That’s why I killed it. It was too funny. Presidents shouldn’t be that funny.

And one of the things that was very striking when Obama spoke at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner was he was that funny. He said the thing you couldn’t believe a president had said. They were often hilarious, but often sometimes too funny. Did you have qualms about that?

Chait: No, I don’t. I think there’s a belief that some people have that humor and insight and dignity are in tension with each other, and I’ve just never thought that. I’ve always thought of humor as an aspect of intelligence. When someone can say something funny, to me that’s a sign that they have some insight that they’re able to express into the world. And I’ve never objected to any figure of any persuasion being funny. [Senator] Ted Cruz, with whom I disagree on almost everything, can often be very, very funny, and I appreciate that about him. I think we need more of it.

Frum: Well, let me quote the Obama joke that made me most uncomfortable, but that was very funny.

So I believe this was the White House Correspondents’ Dinner just after he had been reelected in 2012, and he was taking a bit of a victory lap, and he mentioned that one particular donor, I think it was Sheldon Adelson, had spent the then-astonishing sum of $100 million to defeat him. And Obama, sort of exulting that it hadn’t worked, said: If he felt that strongly about it, why didn’t he just offer the $100 million to me and ask me to leave politics altogether? I’m not saying I would’ve done it, but I would’ve thought about it. And that was really funny, but it’s—

Chait: It’s a great joke.

Frum: It’s a great joke, but why is it a great joke? So, there’s a theory that humor is how we adjust discomfort. It’s how we deal with the taboo and discuss the taboo in a way that’s socially acceptable.

And so the taboo there is, yeah, politicians could bribe rich people. We’ve reached a degree of wealth in American society where a rich man could say: You know, I don’t like your views. Here’s $10 million. Go to an island. I want you never to be heard from again. And there are politicians who might say, Satchel full of money, airplane ticket in hand, off I go. And when you joke about it, you remind people of that reality. Which we all know, but it’s a little uncomfortable to face.

Chait: Or that we’re still banning bribery—at the time, we were still banning bribery. We no longer are banning bribery anymore. But you can spend $100 million. So there’s this last barrier against a rich man’s influence that we can’t cross. So he can go all this way, but he can’t just take the most direct possible route to his ambition.

Frum: So you wrote this book about Obama at the very end of the Obama presidency. Trump came to office. You attracted a lot of attack for the book, because how could you say Obama was effective when he was immediately followed by Trump? You spent a lot of the 2010s defending Obama from critics on the right who said he was a communist and a Kenyan, or a Kenyan communist, or a communist Kenyan. Now the attacks seem to come from the left. I know you’re not a person of tender sensibility, but how do you deal with this?

Chait: You know, it is interesting, and I have reflected on this, because I would say 75 to 80 percent of the argument I make in the book is against those critics on the right, and maybe 20 percent is against the criticisms of the left. And there were criticisms from the left of Obama at the time, but they were just much, much less important.

And what’s interesting in retrospect, as you sort of indicated, is that the conservative critiques have mostly been forgotten, dropped altogether. They’ve just moved on to other things to anger them at the moment. Whereas the left-wing criticisms have survived. They’ve just been repeated over and over again and have established themselves as kind of official histories of that era and are widely believed, even if they weren’t widely believed at the time. And it’s really been fascinating, and I don’t quite have a full handle on how that happened other than just the sheer power of repetition at the time.

In other words, to listen to people talk about Obama now, you would think that Obama was just leaving on the table all these left-wing victories he could have been taking because he was just such a neoliberal shill. That he, out of cussedness, just hated Medicare for All and loved Wall Street.

But at the time, he was seen as a socialist. And it wasn’t just by the Republican Party. The mainstream media was portraying him as a radical. Let me just give you one example—and there are many examples of this—but the kind of official history we have now of the stimulus is that Obama held down the size of the stimulus because he didn’t want to spend more money on stimulus, because he was worried about the deficit. The truth is that Obama, rightly or wrongly, was trying a strategy to get the maximum stimulus sum he thought he could get out of Congress. And Obama was being seen at the time as being completely irresponsible in pursuing stimulus. The New York Times was treating the deficit as the big crisis and the economic crisis as a secondary problem. It was treating his attempt to stimulate the economy in the face of these deficits as perverse. It was basically running stories saying: We are looking at $100 trillion dollar deficits down the road, and nonetheless, Barack Obama wants to spend even more money. Which is such a hard sell. That was the mainstream narrative that he was fighting against, and the whole context in which he was operating has been completely forgotten.

Frum: Well, we were there. And it is true that Obama’s first job as president was saving the banking system and the larger American free-enterprise economy. And maybe he didn’t love that job, but that was the job that history gave him, and that’s what he did.

I have a very unusual view on this, which is I actually think that the period from October 2008 to March of 2009—the Bush-Obama transition—is actually one of the finest hours in the history of U.S. government and the finest hours in the history of the presidency. And a remarkable testimony to two men of different backgrounds working together on a common enterprise in ways that were very generous.

And the one I think about the most was one of the questions that George W. Bush faced in the fall of 2008 was: Should he save General Motors or not? And there were two obvious choices. One was save General Motors, and do it, and then your predecessor would have to live with it. And the other was, kill General Motors, and then your predecessor would have to live with it. And Bush instead made the decision, save them for 90 days, or prob—well, I would forget the exact number of days, but save them for enough of a period that your successor would have full autonomy to decide for himself whether to save General Motors or not. And indeed, we didn’t have a Great Depression, and we didn’t have the collapse of democratic systems all over the world, and we didn’t have a collapse of world communism, er, world capitalism. We didn’t have global communism. I think of those as good things.

Chait: And do you remember the phrase that conservatives applied to the bailout of GM? Gangster. Gangster government was the most common one. Gangster government. This was them indicating that he had gone beyond—they’d already called him a socialist. Now he had gone so far beyond socialism they needed an even viler epithet to describe what he was doing. That these dangerous methods he would use to leverage control of the private sector and basically put us on the road toward communism and improper uses of government power.

Frum: I remember very vividly a conversation I had sometime in the spring of 2009 with a group of young, I think they were Koch fellows or some kind of group funded by conservative projects. And I was much more in the conservative world in those days than I am now, although well on my way out because of this. I remember talking to this group of four or five young people, and they were explaining that if it had been up to them, they would’ve allowed the banks to liquidate themselves.

So I said, Let’s play that out. And I walked them through—I won’t take time here to do it—but, what happens if you allow a bank liquidation? And that means all kinds of people who had good assets suddenly find they don’t have liquidity sufficient to cover their assets. So even though the assets are perfectly fine, they have to be liquidated hastily to raise capital. And you have this accelerating crisis through the whole economy, which is the story of 1931, ’33. But I played it out for them in very vivid terms. And I remember one of them, as I described this nightmare scenario, getting quite ashen and saying: Well, I guess it’s a good thing we weren’t in power then, because our ideas wouldn’t have worked in an emergency.

Chait: Right.

Frum: Well, if your ideas don’t work in an emergency—all the ideas work in nonemergency. (Laughs.) Everything works when it’s not an emergency. The test of your ideas: Does it work when it is an emergency?

Chait: No; I’ve always been taken by that comment because what it’s saying is that our ideas are just a theological commitment. More of an aspiration and not something that you can actually trust to work in the real world. But nonetheless, that we should be guided by them for theological reasons and not for practical ones.

Frum: One of the legacies of that Obama experience was—so the Obama stimulus was about $800 billion, if I remember correctly. About half of it in the form of immediate cash relief and about half of it in the form of spending, which was a big number at the time.

In the Democratic world, that experience was remembered as: Obama didn’t do enough. And so Biden, who was confronting not a deflationary crisis the way Obama was, but an inflationary crisis, he spent much more and ran even bigger deficits—well, maybe they weren’t bigger deficits to the economy, because the government’s revenue hadn’t collapsed as much. But he ran very big deficits. And of course, this time the voices of conventional wisdom were correct; that Biden was spending too much, and he had overlearned the Obama experience that Obama had handled successfully and Biden handled less successfully.

Chait: Obama understood that he needed to stimulate the economy more. I mean, as soon as he got the stimulus, he tried to get more stimulus. He got every dollar he could get out of Congress. You could make an argument that he could have gotten more if he tried different methods, but he was trying to get—he understood, first of all, the recession was deeper than they grasped at the time they passed the stimulus. So they calculated the size of the hole, and they figured out, Okay, so how close to filling up the hole can we get? And then it turns out the hole was even deeper than they thought. So then, they immediately were trying to get more money, and they did get more money. They got more tax credits; they pulled out more stimulus here and there. But they did not get enough stimulus, and the recovery was too slow. And that was the main lesson, that they needed to not repeat that mistake. But the problem is they just erred in the opposite direction under Biden.

Frum: So the left theory of the Obama presidency is: Obama didn’t do enough, and therefore the working class got mad, and they voted for Trump, and it’s Obama’s fault.

Chait: I mean, you can explain Trump’s victory through normal political arguments. You don’t need to summon this crisis of capitalism that produced Trump. It’s hard to win a third consecutive term for any party.

Hillary Clinton was a less talented politician than Obama. She was challenged from the left by Bernie Sanders, and her response to that challenge was for herself to move leftward still. So the candidate who ran in 2016 under difficult conditions for any candidate was not running as Obama’s third term. But she was running significantly to the left of Obama’s third term with less political skills.

Obama left office with a 60 percent approval rating. Obama, had he been able to run for president for a third time, would’ve wiped the floor with Donald Trump. There’s just no reason to believe that Donald Trump was a repudiation of Obama, who was and is very popular, and far more popular than Trump.

Frum: I have a really brain-dead theory of what happened that ignores all the personalities and so on.

Which: This is my theory of how Obama led to Trump. The economy returns to precrisis levels of output and employment in 2014. Pre the crisis of 2007, ’08. So we’re back at 2014 to where we were in 2007, although the growth trajectory is lower. At that point, respectable opinion says: Right; Obama’s been running these big deficits. This could lead to inflation if unchecked. Now is the time for the Federal Reserve to tighten interest rates. And that was not a crazy decision. That’s a very conventional, normal decision. The crisis is over. I mean, we’re back to where we were. Tighten now.

And it turns out the economy was still, in 2014, not healthy yet. And when you tightened in 2014, instead of saying, Okay, the growth continues, as it did when you tightened in the middle ’80s, instead what happened is: The employment growth slows. And so you have very not-recessionary conditions in 2015, 2016, but disappointing conditions. People do not feel continuing improvement, and they weren’t just grateful to be pulled from the sea to the shore. They wanted to resume the normal, you know, trajectory from the shore. And that didn’t happen. And so the incumbent party lost, and then the Federal Reserve recognized its mistake, loosened in 2016, and the economy accelerated in 2017, 2018, 2019. We had three good years before the COVID pandemic.

Chait: Right. They thought we were at capacity. There was a debate about: Are we at capacity? Are we about to hit the point of accelerating inflation in 2014? And we weren’t, and we found that out in Trump’s first term that there was actually plenty of slack left in the labor market, plenty of room to grow.

You’re right. That was an important moment. And that could well have made the difference, because the 2016 election was so close. Just a little bit more growth in those last two [years] could have made the difference. A lot of things could have made the difference.

But I would just point out in the overall macro-situation, Obama was popular. Obama’s popularity was not the problem. I mean, if he was even more popular, it would’ve helped more, but he was overall popular.

Frum: Now in 2026, we have this attack on Obama from the left. He’s now become quite a demon figure. And explain to me—what is the left case in 2026 against Obama? Why is Obama now bad?

Chait: Well, the main thing that they will say that Obama did badly was bailing out the banks in 2008. Obama’s 2008 bank bailout—

Frum: 2009. 2009.

Chait: No, no, no; 2008. Now, of course, the bank bailout did occur in 2008.

Frum: Yeah.

Chait: But Obama did not become president ’til 2009. But when I point this out, people will never believe me. I’ve been pointing this out for 15 years, and no one will believe me. So I think I just have to accept that I’m wrong, and that Barack Obama actually was president in 2008, and he’s therefore responsible for the bank bailout that occurred in 2008.

Frum: I think the bank bailout was good. And whoever was president in 2008—which turns out to be maybe a more difficult question than … I’m sorry to have interrupted you, because I thought it was an easy question. But as you say—as with the question, Who was president in 2020?—it turns out to be quite hard.

Chait: Yes. (Chuckles.)

Frum: So leaving aside the mysterious question of who was president in 2008, why is it, if you’re the left and you love [President] Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who saved the banks, why do you hate whoever was president in 2008, who saved the banks?

Chait: Yeah. I’ve brought up this point many times. It’s very hard for me. I want to faithfully reproduce their criticisms; I don’t want to just be battling straw men. But it’s very hard for me on this point, because I feel like so little sense can be drawn from the criticisms they make. Like I said, the No. 1 point they make is the bank bailout. That’s by far the most common critique they make of Obama. The second most common they make is failing to jail anyone for the crimes of the financial crisis.

What actually happened was, [the Obama administration] looked at it and said: Well, they didn’t commit any crimes. The problem is all this stuff was legal, so we need to change the laws. And so they passed the Dodd-Frank financial reforms, which were the strongest regulations of Wall Street since the 1930s. At the time, those reforms were celebrated by progressives. If you ask any of the progressive experts in financial regulation, they will say that’s a very powerful law; a set of reforms that were formative. It looked at all the problems of the financial crisis, really regulated all of them. It also created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. But [critics] blame Obama for not imprisoning anyone for activity that was only subsequently made illegal. So again, I’m sort of attacking arguments that sound like straw men, but these really are the most common attacks made on Obama.

Frum: Go, take a step beyond the attacks. Because often when people say things, they are applying imperfect words to deep feelings. Okay, so maybe they don’t have good rationalizations, but where does it come from? What is the mentality that says, I revere Franklin Delano Roosevelt, but I hate Barack Obama? Where does that mood come from? Where does, where does Bernie Sanders-ism, what is the emotional need that it meets?

Chait: I think there was significant difference between Obama and the organized progressive movement. Do you remember when Obama’s spokesman derided the professional left? That was a somewhat notorious comment, but it really did capture a hostile relationship between the organized progressive movement and the Obama administration. And he thought that these organized progressive lobbies were unrealistic, didn’t have good ideas, and he had better ideas for messaging and for policy strategy. So they were always on the outs with him, and they resented that.

Biden, by contrast, was so deeply enmeshed with the progressive movement—the “professional left,” as they were called under the Obama era—that it was almost impossible to draw any distance between them at all. Biden did whatever they wanted. And so even though Biden had dramatically less legislative success, the progressive movement really celebrated Biden’s administration all the way ’til the end, when they decided that now Gaza was the only thing that mattered, and Gaza was the reason that he was a failure. But really, up until that moment they were celebrating Biden as the heir to Roosevelt. Biden as the progressive hero, and Obama as the sad, weak appendage to the Reagan era.

Frum: Is there something going on, too, that if you’re on the real left that you regard Trump as not the worst possible outcome? Because if you’re on the real left, Trump is obviously—it isn’t that they like him, but they know the working class, they will sooner or later see through the folly of Trump.

So all we have to do is eliminate the false messiahs and then give them our true messiah, and then they will see through the right and turn to the true messiah. And in fact, an interval of right-wing government maybe—or a Trump government, whether you call it right wing—is a necessary step in the process. Just as Hitler led to the triumph of communism in Germany, so—not to compare Trump to Hitler—but this is the thinking. The far right gets its turn; then we get our turn. We just need to exclude the middle, and then we win.

Chait: This was also the thinking of the communist left in Weimar Germany, right? They saw Hitler’s constituency as their own constituency. They really thought that there was this fluidity between the far left and the far right. I don’t think that was correct at all.

Frum: But at the intellectual level, there’s something to that. I mean, we all know people, and we could name them if we wanted to, who do seem to move very easily between far left and far right. And these are people who are very well educated, who care a lot about politics, care a lot about ideas. You’ll hear them say: I’m a progressive, but I feel at home when I talk to these ultra-MAGA people. We both hate bankers, we both hate Ukraine, we both hate Israel. We have so much in common. And they think, and that must apply at the voting level, where people vote for reasons that are less ideological.

Chait: That’s right. It’s the same error. And that’s why in some level, you’re right that Trump’s election filled them with hope. That they really saw this proletarian uprising that they’ve been longing for but were dejected that was not happening, finally glimmers of it happening. Because you could see elements of Trump’s populist rhetoric as reflecting their own. So I think you’re spot on on that observation.

Frum: So how much of your life do you spend defending the Obama legacy to people who want to detract it, from the left?

Jonathan Chait: Too much. Too much. I’m planning to write something maybe early next year. I’ve gotta just put it all in one place. But It’s gotten to the point where I have this alternate history that only I and a handful of deranged lunatics are aware of. And we’re living in an alternate universe in which everyone else has settled on a completely different interpretation of what happened during those years.

So I’ve gotta just put it all in one place, I think.

Frum: Well, let me ask you about your native Michigan now, because these issues are being played out in real time. Why is the Michigan Senate race, in your view—so much attention was focused on Maine. Now Maine is fading from the center of the discourse. The camera is swiveling to Michigan. Why is that Senate race so important?

Chait: There’s a Democratic Senate primary. Abdul El-Sayed is the left-wing candidate. Haley Stevens is sort of the mainstream center-left candidate. They’re both—

Frum: And is there an incumbent senator in Michigan?

Chait: No. Gary Peters is the incumbent Democrat who’s retiring, so there’s an open seat.

Frum: How competitive a state is Michigan?

Chait: It’s a slightly blue state, although Trump won it in 2024 and in 2016. So it’s very close at the presidential level. Democrats have usually won the Senate races and have usually won the gubernatorial races most of the time, but Donald Trump did win it a couple times. And it’s close enough that the Democrats could lose a Senate seat even in a wave year if they really screw things up. And they seem to at least be putting that possibility on the table.

Frum: So now there’s an open Democratic nomination. There is a Republican candidate who’s competed before, who’s a strong candidate, who’s not a loony at all.

Chait: Right.

Frum: And the Democrats will soon vote to choose one of two candidates. So tell us about the two Democratic choices.

Chait: There’s Haley Stevens, who’s a kind of center-left traditional Democrat. Who would basically—if you took all the Democrats who have won Senate races in Michigan in the last 30 years and put them in a blender and poured them out, you know, you would get Haley Stevens. She’s just an amalgamation of the traditional center-left Democratic Party in the state of Michigan.

Abdul El-Sayed is very left wing for the Democratic Party. He would be the most left-wing Democrat in the Senate, I think even to the left of Bernie Sanders. He would be as far left maybe as people like [U.S. Representatives] Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib. He’s just across-the-board left on every issue, and has really emphasized opposition to Israel as a campaign theme. But he’s trying to do what [former Senate candidate] Graham Platner seemed to be on the road to doing in Maine. But I think he’s even doing it in a more confident, ideologically confident fashion. And he said that if he wins the primary and wins the general election, he is going to start carrying out purges of other Democrats who he thinks can be beaten in primaries.

Frum: And he seems to be a less psychologically troubled person than Graham Platner. And although this is maybe invidious to say, probably more intelligent than Graham Platner.

Chait: I actually have come to question some of his political judgment recently. I feel like he’s played this shrewdly but aggressively, really pushing up against the edge of how much he can get away with. But I feel like recently, it’s like a gambler who’s on a winning streak and is just overplaying his hands.

I’ll give you an example. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed Haley Stevens over the weekend.

Frum: Gretchen Whitmer is the governor.

Chait: The popular governor of the state of Michigan. Popular with Democrats and popular with voters on the whole. If you’re El-Sayed, you just want to just take your lump and walk away from it, right? You want to minimize the impact of this. This is not going to be a good story for you. The only question is how much attention it’s going to get.

But then he goes and attacks Gretchen Whitmer. He takes a shot at her management of the roads, which was one of her original campaign slogans, just fixing the roads, and says the roads haven’t been fixed. So now you’ve given every reporter covering this race a license to extend the story and write about El-Sayed’s vendetta against Whitmer, and you’ve invited Whitmer to weigh into the race once again on Stevens’s behalf. And her approval rating among Democrats, I think, is 88 percent. So you have a tiny number of Democrats who agree with El-Sayed that Gretchen Whitmer is a corporate sellout, which he also thinks and has been saying. But the vast majority love her.

So he’s managed to skate by without really bringing to the surface the degree to which he rejects the entire Democratic Party and its entire philosophy. And he’s trying to get a lot of loyal Democrats to his side, who just want someone who will fight harder against the Republicans and don’t fully understand the ideological extremism that he is bringing to the table.

Frum: Why is this a story outside Michigan? So Democrats may be about to nominate someone who’s more to the left and has a high level of personal aggression and really, really, really hates Israel. And that’s issue No. 1 for him, how much he hates Israel. So suppose he wins. Why is this a story outside Michigan?

Chait: His plan is he will then become the leader of the left. And he said this, and a lot of other leftists have said this, that he will become their standard-bearer. Bernie Sanders is getting old now. And if [El-Sayed] can win, he will prove something that they’ve never been able to demonstrate before—that a left-wing candidate can win in a purple state. You’ve had DSA candidates winning in New York City. You have Bernie Sanders up in Vermont, which is a little bit idiosyncratic. And you have some other House candidates, you have some mayors, but you’ve never had anyone in a purple state winning on a platform this far left. And while El-Sayed is not in the DSA, he is supported by the DSA and he is aligned with the positions of a lot of DSA candidates. So that will completely change the perception of what is electable within the Democratic Party.

Frum: One of the things that matters outside Michigan is the left has probably given away the Maine Senate seat. Susan Collins looks like, at this point, if you had had to guess, she’d probably survive even in Maine, a mostly blue state, even in—

Chait: I’m not sure I agree. It’s a chance. There’s a chance. It’s at risk.

Frum: But something that should’ve been an easy pickup is now very contested.

Michigan is also very—again, as you say, a blue state, but one that does elect Republicans—also could be at risk. Is there any way to a Democratic Senate majority without both Maine and Michigan?

Chait: No. No, I don’t think there is. And the truth is, if you want to think about it from a politically sophisticated perspective, Michigan should have been an easy, easy hold, right? In a blue wave, off-year election, a state that almost always elects Democrats to the Senate—not by huge margins, but pretty reliably by three or four points—should have been an easy hold. And the outcome that I think a lot of moderates are afraid of is that El-Sayed runs, say, four points behind the national Democratic Party. Underperforms due to his extremism, but still gets in because it’s such a huge wave. And then the left turns around and says, See? This shows that our agenda is popular, and we need to implement it everywhere all the time.

Frum: And so then the Democrats lose in 2028 to J. D. Vance and his program of Orbánism in the English language.

Chait: Right. This is going to become the main proof point that’s being used in this interfactional war within the Democratic Party. So if El-Sayed wins, it will be the proof point that the Democratic Party needs to run as far as it can to the left, and that will not impair their ability to win the election in 2028. And I think actually is going to be quite important in terms of the presidential outcome in 2028. In fact, it might even be El-Sayed himself, because they are so enthusiastic about his candidacy. He could, like Obama, [who] went from a first-year senator to presidential candidate, El-Sayed could easily be on that trajectory. That’s how powerful he’s become within the movement so quickly.

Frum: Well, you know, people worry about the loss of consensus in American life and the polarization. But if you have an “El-Sayed versus J. D. Vance” ticket in 2028, at least we can have a consensus about the danger of the Jews. That would be—

Chait: (Laughs.) That’s right.

Frum: America could be united. The two parties could agree on something.

Chait: Right. And then Bloomberg will run a third-party race and get 2 percent, all Jewish vote.

Frum: So what’s at stake here is not just the 2026 outcome but the 2028 outcome as well.

Chait: I think that’s correct; yeah. Yeah, so it’s tremendously consequential.

Frum: So I’m gonna ask you a somewhat personal question, and forgive me if I overstep here. But one of the reasons why Republican moderates lost first to the Tea Party and then to Trump—and there was very little resistance to the Tea Party; there was a lot of resistance to Trump, but it was overwhelmed—was that people of moderate views understandably have moderate personalities. They don’t like conflict. They don’t like trouble. They always believe in compromise, that you can work things out.

And so you get these kinds of soft—you have moderate ideas backed by soft personalities. Fred Siegel—who is a great urbanist, used to be at the Manhattan Institute—had this praise of Rudy Giuliani. And whatever you think of Rudy Giuliani personally, this is, I think, a great phrase. He described Giuliani as “an immoderate centrist.” Which is: He had centrist views, but he was just, he was full of aggression.

Chait: Which eventually won out over the centrism.

Frum: Yeah. So that I think you’ve—this is the part that I was going to put you in. I mean, you are kind of an immoderate centrist. You’re ready to—you have centrist views, but you’re ready to brawl.

Chait: Pugilistic.

Frum: But do you see, as you look at the Democratic Party, that there’s something about the moderate—they will not fight back? And therefore, they’re abdicating by default to people who are going to end up empowering Trump. And whoever Trump’s successor is, probably J. D. Vance, and all that J. D. Vance means for the future of American democracy.

Chait: Absolutely. Look, it’s, it’s an old problem, right? The definition of a liberal is someone who’s too broad-minded to take his own side in an argument. This has been something that liberals have noticed about ourselves and have been complaining about ourselves, without doing anything to change, for generations.

You know, you can find historical exceptions. Sometimes we point to the post–World War II moves by Arthur Schlesinger and Walter Reuther to form Americans for Democratic Action, to exclude the communists, to keep the communists out of the New Deal coalition. And to fight for civil rights and fight for the New Deal values.

But that’s maybe more the exception than the rule in some ways. I mean, there really is something inherent to liberalism, that’s necessary to liberalism. Which is an openness to critique—to not want to become so confident in yourself that you shut out all challenges, right? So I think there is a strength to that quality of liberalism that allows us to be supple, to change our positions with new facts. And I think has made liberalism enduring.

Frum: Where is Obama in all of this? It’s his legacy that is under attack. Both institutionally, but also quite personally. Will he stand up for himself in an argument? Why doesn’t he make himself heard? In a lot of these states, if the choice is Bernie Sanders versus random local Democratic official, Bernie Sanders may win. If it’s Bernie Sanders versus Obama, we know how that fight goes. Is it because he’s an ex-president and doesn’t want to return to the muck and mire of politics? Where is he?

Chait: I think he’s calculated that he can have the most influence by operating behind the scenes. And you’ll notice that the Bernie people absolutely despise Obama, specifically not just for his presidency, but for his role in 2020, right? When you had this sudden coordination of the non-Bernie opposition. The Bernie Sanders strategy in 2020 was to win the Democratic nomination with under 50 percent, by just having his opponents stay divided all the way through the convention. And he would never have to win a Democratic Party majority, and he could get the nomination anyway. And then all of a sudden, just everyone realized they couldn’t win and dropped out and endorsed Biden. And Obama played a role there, and they hate him for that.

So Obama will take an active role, but he doesn’t want to play this factional leadership role that Bernie Sanders plays, where he goes into every contested primary and endorses the most left-wing candidate. I think he’s calculated that will reduce his ability to influence people across the party. That will just make him a much more narrow factional figure. That doesn’t seem like a crazy calculation to me. I can’t say for sure it’s right, though.

Frum: I’m reading, this summer, Kai Bird’s new biography of Roy Cohn, which is—

Chait: Oh, so am I.

Frum: Oh, okay. so if you’re reading the book, you’ll know what I mean. And one of the anecdotes that Bird tells in this book is how President Eisenhower kept coming up with very convincing, very ingenious, plausible arguments for not taking on [Senator] Joe McCarthy directly.

And the first time he says it, and the second time he says it, you think, You make a point. The third and fourth time, you begin to think: You’re just unwilling—possibly you’re scared, but you’re unwilling to take the risk. And actually you’re not acting for good statesmanlike motives. You’re acting for self-preservationist and maybe unworthy motives. When McCarthy starts to attack the Army and to attack Eisenhower’s friends—not just George Marshall, whom he attacked in ’52—but he attacks John J. McCloy in ’53 and ’54. And Eisenhower keeps trying to do things indirectly and has some success. Partly because McCarthy is a desperate alcoholic and becoming very sick. But if McCarthy had not been a desperate alcoholic, it’s not clear that Eisenhower’s methods would’ve worked so well, and he just was making things easy for himself. And I wonder whether with all the subtlety and ingenuity you attribute to Barack Obama, whether he’s also just trying to make things easy for himself.

Chait: You might be right. I’m trying to explain what I think his calculation is. I can’t say for sure that the alternative course of action wouldn’t work, that if he really was willing to fight back and defend his legacy. You know, he does do it in bits and pieces. But he really has allowed the left to win this argument about his legacy, and he hasn’t put up much of a fight.

I mean, I was making the point during his presidency that his support for education reform, which was really something he cherished, began to disintegrate when the teachers’ unions and the left fought back against it, and he just kind of let them do it. And he didn’t defend it, and by the time Hillary Clinton came along, it was really no longer viable ground or defended in the Democratic Party. So I think you’re right that there is this passivity.

Frum: When you say, That’s what he thinks will work. One of my rules of politics is, in fact, none of us know what, what will work. We are always guessing, and we’re usually looking in the mirror and projecting our own wishes. We’re very poor judges of what will work.

But we can be very good judges of what’s the right thing to do. And we also can be, if we really look inward—we know when our reluctance to take a risky action is prompted by truly a prudential calculation. And when there’s just a certain element of, Oh, it’ll be a lot of trouble, a lot of hardship. It’ll be easier for me if I take the softer course. And now I will talk, persuade myself, well—the softer course is also the smart decision. But we never know what the smart decision is. We only know what the right decision is.

Chait: I can’t improve on that.

Frum: Wow. Well, that’s very collegial. (Laughs.)

Jonathan Chait, thank you so much. I’ve got to pocket the rare Chait positive review and put it into my pocket.

Chait: Thank you. I’ll find something to criticize you. Don’t worry. (Laughs.)

Frum: Okay. I know. (Laughs.) Thanks so much for joining me today.

Chait: Thank you, David.

Frum: Bye-bye.

[Music]

Frum: Thanks so much to Jonathan Chait for joining me today on The David Frum Show. As I mentioned at the top of the program, my book this week is a work of history—1177 BC: The Year Civilization Collapsed, by Eric Cline. Published in 2014 by Princeton University Press.

Now, I have not yet seen The Odyssey. I may be alone on my block. It sounds wonderful, and I’m keen to get to it. But one of the things that I am remarking with admiration is that as people have gone to see The Odyssey, they have become fascinated by this question of the transition from one period of civilization to another. A character, I think it’s Odysseus himself, says in the movie, “Our age of bronze is collapsing.” Which is maybe a little on the nose for movie dialogue, but is right.

The Odyssey is a story set in the Bronze Age, written in the Iron Age, measured by which metal was the predominant metal that went into weapons of war and other kinds of tools. And there was a big collapse in between the two. And Eric Cline’s book 1177: The Year Civilization Collapsed is a study of the collapse and an attempt to explain why it happened.

As I understand, and again, I haven’t seen the movie, but the great theme of Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey is that this collapse is, first and foremost, a moral collapse. One civilization has had the kind of life energy seep out of it and is giving way to a new and successor civilization that will be guided by different rules and different values.

And indeed, there really was, across the eastern Mediterranean, a remarkable collapse around the year 1177 B.C. The Hittite Empire—which was the superpower of the time based in what is now southern Turkey—that vanished entirely, and its capital disappeared. Across the Mediterranean, city-states vanished. The Minoan civilization vanished. The New Kingdom in Egypt didn’t quite vanish, but it lost a lot of its military power and never again exerted the kind of power over the region that it had before about the year 1200. Mycenaean Greece, which is where the the characters in The Iliad and The Odyssey supposedly come from, that civilization utterly collapsed. It even lost the ability to read and to write for hundreds of years, only to reemerge later as an Iron Age civilization. And so it is, through up and down the Levant, into the islands, Cyprus.

So what happened? Eric Cline tries to give us an answer. But the key thing to keep in mind, as to the background that enabled all this is that bronze, which is the weapon that the heroes of The Iliad and The Odyssey used for, the metal that they used for their weapons. And that was the main form of armor and tools.

Bronze is a compound of copper and tin. So copper was relatively abundant in the Mediterranean world. There were copper mines in Cyprus and in other places. But tin was scarce in that part of the world and had to be brought to be united with the copper from very far-flung places—as far as Cornwall in Great Britain and Afghanistan in the center of Asia.

So when you’re committed to bronze, you’re committed to very global trade routes. And because the trade routes are so extended, you build large states. Because you have large states, you need ways to manage the states, including organized religion and reading and writing and some kind of numbering system. How do you keep track of how much tin has moved from Afghanistan to Babylonia, and when it moved, and who moved it? You need some form of writing. And you need a bureaucracy. You need comparably sophisticated and elaborated states.

Something happened around the year 1177 [B.C.E.], and Cline makes a good case that it’s a compound of ecological effects. Droughts and earthquakes that weakened the states, ended their ability to import tin, reduced the availability of the bronze alloy made from copper and tin, and set these states reeling backward and made them militarily vulnerable to invaders and small bands that otherwise they would’ve just brushed off with superior strength.

Through the Bronze Age, people knew about iron. But iron was a more difficult material to work. In particular, it required a lot of heat. And it just seemed that bronze—which was easier to work with and had a lot of prestige attached to it—that that was the natural metal of choice. But once the bronze is no longer available because the tin has become hard to get, people are forced back to figure out ways to work with the iron. And once they do so, they find that iron is a dramatically superior weapon of war. Makes sharper, stronger swords, spears, and arrowheads. And so iron replaces it, and the world never looks backward to bronze. Bronze is from then on used primarily for statuary and art, because it remains a prestige material, but it’s not a workable material.

But the Cline story is one of environmental change leading to material innovation, not a story of moral decay. It wasn’t that people somehow lost faith in themselves and therefore turned away from bronze, and then found a new faith and therefore turned to iron. They had very practical problems. Now, I don’t want to dispute the importance to art of telling stories about moral decay and moral regeneration. But as we’re trying to understand why civilizations actually change, I mean, morality surely plays a part in it. Anyone watching the crisis of American democracy right now has to face that the greatness of a society and the ebb of greatness can be attributed to moral defects in that society.

But we also need to pay a lot of attention to ecological changes that force change upon society, and to the material responses to environmental change. Because while we’re not doing a great job in 21st-century America to adapting to our moral challenges, we’re doing an even worse job of adapting to climate changes. And if climate is what felled the Hittites, and as other historians will tell us, if climate is what felled the Romans, and if climate is what, as other historians again tell, felled the Ming Empire and led to the rise of new civilizations in China—then climate, if we don’t pay attention to it, it could be the falling of us.

So as we enjoy the movie, as we absorb its powerful moral lessons, we also need to keep our eye on the material world, the world of climate and weather. Maybe we can’t control it, but we’d best learn to adapt to it. Because if we don’t, it will be the end of us.

Thanks so much for watching The David Frum Show this week. I hope you will share the program and like it on whatever platform you use. As ever, if you’re minded to support the program, the best way to do so is by subscribing to The Atlantic and support all of my colleagues, including my colleague Jonathan Chait. See you next week on The David Frum Show.

Bye-bye.

entries.title: Why Kids Can’t Quit Roblox
entries.summary: The mechanics of many games on the platform are nearly identical to those of slot machines and sports-betting apps.
entries.content:
The mechanics of many games on the platform are nearly identical to those of slot machines and sports-betting apps.

A couple of years ago, Peter Galassi realized that he had a problem: His 9-year-old son was still, somehow, constantly on Roblox, despite the screen-time limits Galassi had set for him. He soon discovered that his son had used his mom’s phone to secretly open multiple accounts on the platform. Why? Because, like a gambler with a fistful of lottery tickets, he wanted to increase his odds in games such as Adopt Me, in which players hatch eggs for a chance to win rare pets.

Every time the boy played, though, he seemed to sink into distress. Fighting games offended his sense of fairness: He was outraged that players could pay to be VIPs, killing everyone within seconds. And watching other players get “lucky” over and over left him in tears. Then came the “apoplectic meltdowns,” three broken tablets, and this devastating refrain: “My luck is horrible; my life is horrible.” It was, Galassi said, like “we had a son who was on meth.”

A tech-savvy Millennial who also games, Galassi had vetted Roblox before allowing his son to play. Roblox itself doesn’t design the games that appear on its platform; it provides creation tools to third-party developers, whose games Roblox then hosts. Galassi’s first impression, as he surveyed the landscape, was: “These games all seem really crappy and boring—I don’t understand what is the appeal.” It wasn’t until he looked again, after his son started throwing tantrums, that he realized something much more complex was going on.

Not all video games are created equal, of course. Some build social connection, boost memory and focus, and even encourage physical activity, Jason Nagata, an associate professor of pediatrics at UC San Francisco, told me. But many of today’s most popular games involve a style of play unlike any that parents might have seen before, if they were raised on Super Mario Bros. and Tetris. The games have cartoony graphics that may look innocuous, especially when compared with hyperrealistic first-person shooters. But in many cases, their design and interactive elements are less Zelda, more Vegas.

Many games that might appear, to the casual observer, to be an obstacle course or a world-building challenge also contain tempting loot boxes: virtual items that players open blind, revealing surprise rewards of varying value. Nearly 60 percent of the top-grossing games on Google Play and iPhone include them. Although they can be earned, they’re also typically available for purchase. The promise of winning rare items—such as limited-edition hats and extra-lethal weapons—may prompt additional spending. It’s like the Pokémon pack-opening craze, in which people buy dozens, sometimes hundreds, of packs hoping to snag a rare card—except that with games on Roblox and other platforms, players need not schlep to the store or even rise from the couch.

Video games have long operated on a system of challenges and rewards. But earning those prizes usually depended on defeating a dragon, solving a maze, unearthing clues. Today’s bounty, by contrast, can be a player’s instantly—if they’re willing to pay for multiple rolls of the dice or a boost of luck.

These mechanics are not incidental. In the games that employ them, they are designed to maximize engagement. And they’re nearly identical to the variable-reward loops that slot machines and sports-betting apps use in games for adults and that research has shown to be particularly addictive. Games that look like simple fun, according to addiction experts I spoke with while reporting this article, may be normalizing behaviors that could lead to serious consequences down the road.

In recent years, since the 2018 Supreme Court decision that overturned a federal ban on sports gambling, researchers and psychiatrists specializing in addiction have argued that the rise in problem gambling has become a more and more urgent public-health concern. Thirty-nine states and Washington, D.C., have legalized sports gambling, to the tune of nearly $167 billion wagered and roughly $17 billion in revenue last year. Prediction markets such as Polymarket and Kalshi, once curiosities primarily for finance and math nerds, are now mainstream. (Both companies have disputed that their prediction-market services are a form of gambling.) Last year, the National Problem Gambling Helpline reported a steady rise in calls to helplines year over year from 2020 to 2024, and a “significant” increase in calls from younger people, ages 13 to 34, from 2023 to 2025. Meanwhile, scientists and regulators are scrambling to understand and mitigate any potential impacts.

All mammals, humans included, are evolutionarily primed to prefer random rewards over predictable ones, Anthony Vaccaro, a psychologist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, told me. It’s a drive that helped our ancestors find the tree with the best fruit or the hunting ground with the most game—and a fact of our nature that can make us inclined to find gambling really, really fun.

Normally, the brain’s control center keeps its reward center in check to curb behavior such as compulsive gambling. But in gambling addicts—and in kids, whose brains are still developing—that balance can tip. “The adolescent brain might be particularly vulnerable to developing problems” such as addiction, Marc Potenza, a psychiatrist and gambling researcher at Yale, told me. That’s because brain regions sensitive to rewards develop earlier than those that exert control. Thus, children’s early exposure to games that emphasize intermittent rewards might derail normal brain development, the thinking goes, leading to a higher risk of addictive behaviors in adulthood.

This pattern has clear analogs in other contexts. Take e-cigarettes: Some studies have found that kids who vaped were “much more likely to become hooked on nicotine” than if they had not vaped, Vaccaro said. Research into whether gambling-like play among video gamers can be linked to problem gambling is still nascent. And it is unclear whether loot boxes inspire gambling or simply attract people already prone to gamble. But some evidence—including analyses of behavioral patterns among people who, as children, played games featuring loot boxes—suggests a connection. One 2023 longitudinal study observed, for example, that young adults who played games with loot boxes were, six months later, more likely to start gambling than those who did not play with loot boxes.

Anna Lembke, a professor and medical director of addiction medicine at the Stanford University School of Medicine, told me that one can look to other patterns of addiction and begin to connect the dots. “There is evidence showing that the earlier that a child is exposed to social media, the more likely they are to get addicted to social media,” she said. “The earlier that they’re exposed to drugs and alcohol, the more likely they are to get addicted to drugs and alcohol. So we can infer from that that the earlier they’re exposed to gambling, the more likely they are to get addicted to gambling.”

Even if loot boxes aren’t creating problem gamblers, Vaccaro told me, exposure matters. When gambling mechanics are embedded in so many games, they end up “capturing more people that would be at risk,” he said. If at age 6 you’ve spent hours in a game hatching eggs compulsively, it could be that in your 20s, throwing some action on a Knicks game might not feel like such a leap. Or, as Galassi told me: “It’s hard for me to not believe that, like, we’re not priming these kids to just dump their money into FanDuel the second they have a checking account.”

Lembke noted that it is important to not overstate the risk. “Typically, the majority of people exposed to an addictive substance do not get addicted to that substance,” she said. “But if you have a substantial-enough minority of folks getting addicted, then you have a public-health problem. I think we’re beginning to recognize that we have a public-health problem when it comes to addiction to all kinds of digital media, including gambling.”

Many parents don’t realize that their children are being ensnared by psychological tricks similar to those that casinos use to hook adults. “They just think, Oh, my kid wants some money to spend in an online game,” Michael Robb, a researcher at Common Sense Media who released a report in January on gambling and boys, told me. But frequent requests such as this could indicate that the games children play are cultivating compulsive behavior.

Many of the parents I spoke with who caught on fastest to these dynamics work in tech fields that employ gambling-like strategies. Tony Nguyen, a digital marketer in Orange County, California, told me that when his 11-year-old son started playing games on Roblox, his personality changed practically overnight. Some mornings, his son would wake up at 5 a.m. to attend “limited drop” events, in which rare items are doled out to participants at random. “He would just sit for all three hours” for a chance to win one skin, a custom outfit for an avatar, Nguyen said. His son also gamed while watching streamers: people playing in real time for a live audience on YouTube, part of an entangled ecosystem of influencers, game developers, and players that keeps kids locked in. These influencers were also popular with Galassi’s son, the Adopt Me aficionado. Galassi shared one video with me, a 19-minute clip. In it, the host, who has 3.64 million subscribers, gets lucky just two minutes in: She squeals as she hatches a turtle, pumps her fist in the air, and chants, “Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes!”

For many, seeing a rare item on a loot-box prize list, surrounded by bright colors and countdown timers, can trigger intense FOMO. A desire for social cachet—players can opt to make their treasured inventory visible to others—also tempts kids to try to land a coveted object. These pressures, coupled with a lack of knowledge about how probability works, can lead to significant financial fallout.

Parents may not notice until a credit card linked to a Roblox account has accrued substantial charges or until a child has begged or traded for one too many gift cards for Robux, the platform’s in-game currency. In a report last year, Fairplay, an advocacy organization working to shield children from exploitative business practices by tech companies, highlighted instances of children racking up thousands of dollars in purchases. “The kid just thinks, I gotta keep clicking until I reach this item,” Haley Hinkle, Fairplay’s policy counsel, told me.

In the United States, these gaming dynamics have largely escaped regulatory scrutiny. Most gambling laws were written for a pre-digital world, which means that loot boxes exist in a “crazy space,” Robb said. Not everyone, for example, considers loot boxes gambling—parents included. And federal law states that something of value must be wagered to qualify as gambling. So loot boxes, whose contents typically can’t be exchanged for money, may not meet this definition—though a robust marketplace of third-party vendors does offer opportunities for players to trade rare items for cash.

Some regulators and legislators are approaching the issue from a consumer-protection angle, the tactic taken in recent lawsuits against Meta and Google, which allege that these companies’ products are addictive and developmentally inappropriate for minors. (Both companies have disputed the lawsuits’ accusations.) Legislators in New York State are considering several loot-box bills that would prevent platforms such as Roblox from offering gambling-like features such as skin cases and pay-to-win transactions on platforms children use. And in May, Fairplay, together with other advocacy groups, asked the Federal Trade Commission to investigate Roblox for unfair and deceptive practices designed to keep kids online and spending. Their request, which the FTC has not yet responded to, argues that the platform’s mechanics—layered currencies obscuring real prices, complex probability calculations that even an adult would find confusing, casino-style visuals, ads bombarding players the moment they log on—cause harm. It also argues that because so many children are on Roblox (in 2024, the company reported that roughly 40 percent of its active daily users were younger than 13), the potential impact on kids is profound. Roblox has stated that it “strongly disputes these claims.”

Complicating questions about who is liable when problems arise is the fact that Roblox doesn’t design its own games. Independent developers, some as young as 13, have created the more than 40 million “experiences,” or games and interactive worlds, available on the platform. Theoretically, developers must follow Roblox’s community standards and creator guidelines, which outline what counts as prohibited types of gambling. But those definitions are both narrow and subjective. Many games may not look exactly like slot machines or roulette wheels, for instance, but they contain imagery that strongly resembles such games, substituting cute characters for coin or playing-card imagery. (AI tools are likely to make it even easier for people to quickly spin up addictive games.) It is also unclear how many developers who skirt the rules will ever face consequences: Potential breaches of the guidelines are largely self-policed, with the company relying on moderators and gamers to report violations.

Roblox, which had $4.9 billion in revenue last year but is not profitable, takes a substantial cut—up to 70 percent—of every in-game item a developer sells to players. So creators must earn, and earn a lot, to see a return, which can influence how they design. They might, for instance, lean more into creating games involving trading and random chance, Taylor Hardwick, a postdoctoral researcher who studied Roblox’s revenue-generating strategies while at the University of Sydney, told me. She was part of a team whose research began as a broad look at Australian children’s spending choices. In one study, the researchers gave 22 children 20 Australian dollars each to spend as they wished. But when half used the money on Robux, the most popular choice by far, the team quickly pivoted their research to an analysis of Roblox itself. She described the “pay to play” ethos on Roblox as “ambient.”

When I asked Roblox about the widespread presence of pay-to-play games on its platform, a spokesperson noted that “only 1.4 percent of our 132 million daily active users were payers” and that it has “clear policies prohibiting both actual and simulated gambling.” It also pointed to its recent rollout of age-based accounts, which it said “bring age checks, content ratings, ongoing game reviews, and parental controls into an easy-to-understand framework for kids, teens, older users, and parents.” Of course, 1.4 percent of daily active users could still be a lot of children, based on the company’s reported number of young users.

Chance-based games and predatory sales practices have plagued other companies that welcome third-party developers, including Minecraft and Fortnite, although Minecraft doesn’t directly profit from these games. Lamar B., a Minecraft player from Kentucky with whom I chatted on Reddit, and who asked that his last name not be used because he feared being harassed online for criticizing the platform, posted that his 10-year-old niece had gambled away her allowance on loot boxes in third-party Minecraft servers, including some appearing under the Official Minecraft Server List. He’d encountered roadblocks when trying to report some loot boxes as offensive content. “Most of the time, you cannot get a human to answer—they have an AI chatbot on their support site,” he told me. Games he reported months ago continue to thrive. When I contacted Minecraft to ask about Lamar’s claims, a spokesperson wrote that the company’s usage guidelines “prohibit gambling-related content, and we take action when experiences violate those standards.”

Hinkle told me that companies trusted to self-regulate sometimes fall short. Roblox’s age checks and expanded parental controls may represent progress, but they don’t address the underlying gameplay mechanics, she said. That would require more substantive structural changes to the way games earn money, which would inevitably cut into companies’ profits. Overall, the global market for in-game purchases is huge—estimated at $81 billion for mobile games in 2024, and $34 billion for games on PCs and consoles last year.

For now, parents must decide where to draw the line. That is possible only with awareness, however. Some parents, such as Galassi and Nguyen, have banned their children from playing any games with gambling-like mechanics. Yet with screens infiltrating many aspects of life, kids have abundant opportunity to play out of sight of even the most vigilant families. Grassroots advocacy groups, such as Parents Standing Together and Parents Together Action, offer support and education. But ultimately, the burden rests with families to set boundaries—and stay alert.
